name: The Longfellow Linden

location.address: Longfellow House-Washington's Headquarters National Historic Site, 105 Brattle Street, Cambridge, MA
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge (within the day-trip boundary of Boston, roughly 20-25 minutes via Red Line to Harvard Square then a short walk)

story: In the summer of 1844 Henry Wadsworth Longfellow came home to find that workmen had "lopped away the long low branches of my Linden tree, misunderstanding my directions", and he wrote it up in his journal as a small catastrophe. The tree outlived him. It went into the ground around 1800 to 1810, planted by Andrew Craigie, who owned the Brattle Street estate before the poet came to it in 1843, and it stands on the East Lawn of a house that had served as George Washington's headquarters during the siege of Boston a generation before the linden existed. Fanny Longfellow wrote in 1843 of wanting "a linden avenue in which my poet intends to pace in his old age". This is the only tree of that avenue still standing. By 1846 he was describing her reading Heine underneath it. The National Park Service puts it at 82 feet, against roughly 60 for the species, with a trunk 84 inches through, and rates its condition fair to poor: the trunk cavity is filled, cables carry the branches, heavy pruning comes round every five years. Since the early 2000s the park has been growing a genetically identical cutting against the day it goes. The grounds are free and open in daylight; only the house tours are ticketed.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime flowers and the whole East Lawn smells of it

access: Free; National Historic Site grounds are open to the public daily during daylight hours (house tours are separately ticketed but the East Lawn where the tree stands is publicly accessible)
transport: MBTA Red Line to Harvard Square, then about 8-10 minutes on foot down Brattle Street

name: The Houghton Beech

location.address: 1000-1008 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA (between Harvard Square and Central Square, on the site of the former Houghton estate, now part of MIT/University Park land)
location.neighbourhood: Cambridge, Mid-Cambridge/University Park (within the day-trip boundary; on the Red Line corridor)

story: This is Cambridge's only living Historic Landmark, and it was made one in 1985 to stop a building. A developer's plans for the site would have taken a third of the copper beech's crown and finished it off, so about thirty neighbours formed a group called the Friends of the Beech Tree and petitioned the city; the Historical Commission designated the tree itself, the legal instrument normally reserved for buildings. The Harvard Crimson, reporting from the October 1985 hearing, called it 203 years old, which puts its planting around 1782 and makes it roughly 240 now. That figure carries more weight than the biography printed around it in the same article, which has Henry O. Houghton serving as mayor decades before he founded the Riverside Press. A 2018 local survey of Cambridge trees offers a looser "planted 150+ years ago", a lower bound rather than a contradiction. Houghton planted three beeches on his family estate here. This is the one left. MIT bought the property in the 1970s and took down the buildings, and the tree stayed, which is how a private estate specimen ended up standing on a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue between Central and Harvard. Most of Boston's notable trees sit inside curated collections. This one you walk past on the way to the bus.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves open translucent red before they darken to purple-black

access: Free; stands beside a public sidewalk on Massachusetts Avenue, fully visible and reachable at any time
transport: MBTA Red Line to Central Square, then about 8 minutes on foot along Mass Ave toward Harvard Square
